sections.heading: What technical communication is
bullets: Definition: transferring technical information so a specific audience can act on it accurately.
Properties: accuracy, clarity, conciseness, completeness, audience-appropriateness.
Channels: written (reports, mail), oral (meetings, demos), visual (diagrams, slides).

sections.heading: Process model
bullets: 7-step flow: defining purpose → analysing audience → selecting & organising content → choosing style/format → drafting → editing/proofreading → delivering.
Audience analysis: expertise level, expectations, resistance — decides jargon, tone, depth.
Purpose split: to inform, to persuade, to instruct, to entertain (technical rarely the last).

sections.heading: Language fundamentals
bullets: Sentence types (simple/compound/complex/compound-complex) — vary them, but prefer short sentences in instructions.
Voice: active for clarity ('The technician switched off the supply'), passive when the actor is irrelevant.
Tense consistency: methods sections stay past; universal facts present.
Common errors: dangling modifiers, faulty parallelism, ambiguous pronoun reference.

questions.prompt: List the 7 steps of the technical communication process in order.
questions.answer: Purpose → Audience → Content/organise → Format/style → Draft → Edit/proof → Deliver
solution: Start with why the document exists.
Audience analysis shapes everything downstream.
Draft then revise — writing IS rewriting.

questions.prompt: Rewrite for clarity: 'The results were obtained by us being conducted in the lab yesterday.'
questions.answer: 'We obtained the results in the lab yesterday.'
solution: Original mixes passive ('were obtained') with dangling agent ('by us being').
Use active voice with a clear actor.
Result: shorter, unambiguous.

questions.prompt: Which channel suits: (a) step-by-step safety procedure (b) quarterly project update?
questions.answer: (a) Written instruction sheet; (b) Oral presentation + one-page summary
solution: Procedures must be referenceable & unambiguous → written, numbered steps.
Updates need dialogue & emphasis → oral, backed by a take-away document.

questions.prompt: Identify the fault: 'After reviewing the report, the data seemed unreliable.'
questions.answer: Dangling modifier — 'the data' did not review the report
solution: The introductory phrase must attach to the subject that performed it.
Fix: 'After we reviewed the report, the data seemed unreliable.' or 'After reviewing the report, we found the data unreliable.'

sections.heading: Oral fundamentals
bullets: Elements: pronunciation, articulation, pitch, pace, pause, stress, intonation.
Pace target ≈ 120–150 words/min; silence after key points lets them land.
Filler control ('um', 'like') — replace with a pause; pausing sounds confident.

sections.heading: Presentation structure
bullets: Rule of three: opening (hook + roadmap), body (3 points max), close (call to action).
One idea per slide; 6×6 heuristic (≤6 words per line, ≤6 lines) as a starting cap.
Signposting: 'First… Next… Finally…' — the audience should always know where they are.
Q&A: listen fully, rephrase, answer, check — never argue with the room.

sections.heading: Voice & body
bullets: Eye contact in triangles (left-back, right-back, centre) — not at the slides.
Gestures above the waist, open palms; avoid pacing and pocketed hands.
Handle nervousness: prepare aloud twice, breathe low & slow, first sentence memorised.

questions.prompt: Design a 3-part opening for a 5-minute project demo.
questions.answer: Hook (problem stat/slide) → Relevance ('why you care') → Roadmap ('3 things I'll show')
solution: Open with tension: a problem the audience feels.
Promise the payoff.
Preview structure so they can follow easily.

questions.prompt: You say 'um' 20 times a minute. Two concrete fixes?
questions.answer: Replace with deliberate pauses; drill the talk aloud twice before presenting
solution: Silence > filler — count 2 beats after every key claim.
Preparation reduces cognitive load where fillers sneak in.

questions.prompt: Ideal speaking pace and words-per-slide guidance?
questions.answer: 120–150 wpm; one idea per slide (≈6×6 words)
solution: Faster than 160 wpm rushes comprehension; slower than 100 drags.
Slides are signposts, not teleprompters — details go in speech or handouts.

questions.prompt: Audience asks a hostile question. Best response sequence?
solution: Rephrasing buys thinking time and disarms hostility by validating the question.
Stay factual; take grudges offline after the session.

sections.heading: Report architecture
bullets: Front matter: title page, abstract/executive summary, table of contents.
IMRaD spine for technical reports: Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion.
Conclusion restates findings without new data; recommendations are actionable (who, what, when).

sections.heading: Style for documents
bullets: Para = one idea (topic sentence + support); 3–5 sentences typical.
Lists for anything enumerable — parallel grammatical structure across items.
Headings are navigation: noun-heavy, scannable ('3. Calibration Procedure' not 'More').
Figures need: number, caption, units, reference in text before appearance.

sections.heading: Mechanics & ethics
bullets: Tense: past for what you did, present for what the data shows.
Numbers: consistent units (SI), consistent decimal places; spell out one–nine at sentence start.
Plagiarism & citation: quote verbatim with quotes; paraphrase + cite; reference manager (Zotero free).
Editing pass order: content → structure → sentences → typos (never the reverse).

questions.prompt: Order the sections of a standard experimental report.
questions.answer: Abstract → Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion → Conclusion → References
solution: Abstract summarises all (write last).
IMRaD is the backbone.
References support every non-original claim.

questions.prompt: Rewrite for parallel structure: 'The task involves collecting samples, analysis of data, and reports are written.'
questions.answer: 'The task involves collecting samples, analysing data, and writing reports.'
solution: All three items must be the same grammatical form (gerunds here).
Parallel lists are easier to scan and remember.

questions.prompt: When must a paraphrased idea be cited?
questions.answer: Always — citing is required even with your own words
solution: Ideas are attributed; only YOUR original analysis goes uncited.
Include page/section and list it in references.

questions.answer: Figure number + descriptive title, units/scale, conditions/legends explained
solution: A figure must be understandable standalone.
Reference it in the body text before it appears.

sections.heading: Professional writing
bullets: Email: informative subject line, BLUF (bottom line up front), scannable body, clear ask + deadline, professional close.
Meetings: agenda before, decisions & owners during, minutes after — 'no action items = wasted hour'.
Bad news: buffer → reason → bad news → close; never bury the ask.

sections.heading: Team & intercultural communication
bullets: Active listening: paraphrase, question, summarise before responding.
Feedback model SBI: Situation–Behaviour–Impact — personalise the behaviour, never the person.
Intercultural: avoid idiom/slang, check understanding, vary communication styles, respect holidays/names.

sections.heading: Engineering ethics
bullets: Core duties: public safety first, competence, honesty, IP respect, confidentiality, conflict-of-interest disclosure.
Indian context: consumer safety, IS standards, data privacy (DPDP Act), no falsification of lab/exam data.
Whistle-blowing ladder: raise internally → documented escalation → authority as last resort.

questions.prompt: Draft a one-line email subject that follows best practice for requesting a lab sign-off.
questions.answer: Action needed: Physics Lab 04 record sign-off by Fri 3 Oct
solution: Include action + object + deadline.
Recipient triages correctly without opening.
Specific beats vague ('Query' or 'Hi' are failures).

questions.prompt: Give feedback to a teammate who missed deadlines, using the SBI model.
questions.answer: Situation: two sprint deadlines; Behaviour: submissions arrived 2 days late; Impact: reviewer time shifted and demo slipped
solution: State observable facts, not labels ('you're careless' → unactionable).
Impact connects behaviour to the team.
End with agreed remedy and follow-up date.

questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to adjust experimental data to 'look consistent'. What do you do?
questions.answer: Refuse — data falsification violates engineering ethics and safety duties
solution: Public safety & honesty outrank hierarchy in every professional code.
Offer legitimate alternatives: more trials, error bars, methodology note.
Escalate through proper channels if pressured.

questions.prompt: List 3 rules for intercultural team emails.
questions.answer: No idiom/slang; short plain sentences; confirm understanding politely
solution: Idioms ('hit it out of the park') don't translate.
Plain English also helps non-native readers at speed.
Ask 'does this match your understanding?' rather than assuming.
